html:
The Cochimí were the Indigenous people of the central Baja California peninsula, from El Rosario in the north to San Javier in the south. They lived in a dry land with little water, moving in small bands between springs and the coast.

They lived by gathering and hunting: agave hearts, cactus fruit, seeds, small game, and shellfish and fish on the coasts. In the Sierra de San Francisco are the Great Murals, huge paintings of people and animals; the Cochimí told the Jesuits these had been made by giants who came before them.

From 1697 Jesuit missionaries founded a chain of missions up the peninsula, and most of what we know of Cochimí customs and beliefs comes from their writings, above all those of Miguel Venegas and Miguel del Barco. Epidemics swept the missions, and by the early 1800s the Cochimí had almost disappeared as a people. Their southern neighbours were the Guaycura.
